sections.body: Citation mapping and discovery is the part of AI research work that treats papers as nodes in a network and asks how ideas move between them. In practice, systems parse reference lists, resolve author and venue names, build citation graphs, and attach metadata such as year, field, and abstract. AI then adds layers that plain counting cannot provide, including paper embeddings for similarity, classifiers for citation intent, and temporal models for how links appear over time. These tools help a reader find related work, trace a method back to its sources, and see when a topic starts to connect to another. The work is operational, not theoretical, and it runs on messy metadata, partial text, and changing publication practices.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this work are settled. Reference parsing, deduplication, and basic graph construction are reliable enough for everyday use, and similarity search over abstracts or full text is common. Citation intent is harder, because a citation can be background, a method borrowed, a result compared, or a criticism, and models still confuse these cases. Trend forecasting is the least stable layer, since early signals are noisy and a burst of papers can reflect funding, fashion, or a new benchmark rather than a durable shift. This site holds 135 research papers, so its maps are a partial view and should be read as a guide to the local library, not as a census of a field. Links go to the original paper, not to a search tool, which lets a reader check the source and judge the context.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants the raw shape of the network should begin with Citation Graphs Over Time, which shows how links accumulate and where clusters form across years. Clustering Papers by Meaning takes a different route, grouping papers by what they say rather than by who cites whom, so it is the page for finding similar work that never shares a reference. How a Paper Is Cited goes deeper into a single edge, explaining citation context and intent, which matters when a link is critical rather than supportive. Bridge Studies Between Fields follows papers that connect separate communities, and it is the place to look for work that imports a method from one area into another. Forecasting Research Trends sits at the end of this chain, using the graph, the clusters, and the bridge points to estimate where attention may move next, with the caveats that the state paragraph describes.
